body_text:
Global Consequences of the Mean Value Theorem. The Mean Value
Theorem is the fundamental conduit translating infinitesimal local
differential information into global functional conclusions:
1. **Constant Function Theorem**: If $f'(x) = 0$ for all
   $x \in (a, b)$, then $f$ is constant on $(a, b)$. For any
   $x_1 < x_2$, there is $c \in (x_1, x_2)$ with
   $f(x_2) - f(x_1) = f'(c)(x_2 - x_1) = 0$.
2. **Monotonicity**: If $f'(x) \geq 0$ for all $x \in (a, b)$,
   then $f$ is monotonically non-decreasing; if $f'(x) > 0$, $f$
   is strictly increasing.
3. **Lipschitz Continuity**: If $|f'(x)| \leq M$ for all
   $x \in (a, b)$, then $|f(x_2) - f(x_1)| \leq M |x_2 - x_1|$ for
   all $x_1, x_2 \in (a, b)$.

The connectedness of the domain interval is strictly required: on
disconnected domains, a function with vanishing derivative can
take distinct constant values on separate components.
